description: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 Aug 1990, removing ~4.3 million bpd combined output from the market and triggering the Gulf War; Brent rose from roughly $17 to a peak near $46 by mid-October 1990.
US-led coalition launched military action to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait; oil prices fell sharply once the war began as supply-disruption fears eased.
Collapse of the Thai baht on 2 Jul 1997 spread across Asia, crushing regional oil demand growth just as OPEC had raised quotas; Brent roughly halved between late 1997 and end of 1998.
Terrorist attacks on the US raised geopolitical risk premiums and contributed to a global economic slowdown that softened oil demand into 2002.
US-led invasion of Iraq began 20 Mar 2003, disrupting Iraqi oil exports and adding a sustained geopolitical risk premium to prices through the 2000s.
Lehman Brothers' bankruptcy on 15 Sep 2008 triggered a global financial crisis; Brent collapsed from a July 2008 peak near $147 to about $40 by December 2008 as demand cratered.
OPEC agreed a series of cuts totalling ~4.2 million bpd between Sep-Dec 2008 in response to the collapsing post-crisis price, helping stabilize the market into 2009.
Widespread uprisings across the Middle East and North Africa, including Libya's civil war starting mid-Feb 2011, removed substantial Libyan output and pushed Brent above $125 by April 2011.
OPEC's 27 Nov 2014 Vienna meeting decided not to cut production despite a global glut driven by US shale growth; Brent fell over $6 in a single day to $71.25 and continued toward $50 by January 2015.
OPEC agreed its first production cut since 2008 on 30 Nov 2016, and non-OPEC producers led by Russia joined on 10 Dec 2016, forming the OPEC+ coalition and helping prices recover from 2014-16 lows.

event_name: US Withdrawal from Iran Nuclear Deal (JCPOA)
description: The US withdrew from the JCPOA on 8 May 2018 and re-imposed sanctions on Iranian oil exports effective 5 Nov 2018, removing Iranian barrels from the market and supporting prices through mid-2018.
OPEC+ talks collapsed on 6 Mar 2020; Saudi Arabia responded with steep discounts and a production surge announced 8 Mar 2020, crashing Brent alongside collapsing COVID-19 demand.

WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 Mar 2020; global lockdowns caused an unprecedented demand shock, with Brent falling to roughly $9-19 per barrel by late April 2020 (WTI briefly went negative on 20 Apr 2020).
OPEC+ agreed a record cut of 9.7 million bpd on 12 Apr 2020, effective 1 May 2020, to counter the COVID-19 demand collapse, helping stabilize and gradually recover prices through 2020-21.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine on 24 Feb 2022 triggered Western sanctions on Russian energy exports and fears of a global supply disruption, pushing Brent above $120 by early March 2022.
